Title: Near to the Wild Heart
Review: Holy Virginia Woolf. Why have I not read more Lispector? Joana is a force of nature, such a vibrant character.

Title: The Reverse Centaur's Guide to Life After AI: How to Think About Artificial Intelligence―Before It's Too Late
Review: I appreciate that in both this and Enshittification, he lays out clear (though not easy) things that ordinary people can do to stand up to the rich who are trying to control everything. His books somehow manage to be both infuriating and encouraging simultaneously.

Title: The Hacienda
Review: Creepy and ferocious. I took a while to warm up to the main character but I related to her confusion – there were many times I didn’t know what was about to happen next! Just as good as Vampires of El Norte, it also takes gothic genre conventions and distorts them just a little so that it’s incredibly satisfying. I love a good gothic manor.

Title: Final Orbit
Review: I’m a sucker for anything NASA and this was good fun. I breezed through it and, while it didn’t always keep me guessing, it was always entertaining.

Title: The Bewitching
Review: I do love a witchy story. This was compelling, though by the third quarter I began to feel it was getting a tiny bit repetitive and could have been wrapped up a little sooner.

Title: Saturday Is for Funerals
Review: A valuable collection of reminiscences from Botswana shortly after the height of the AIDS crisis when ARVs were widely available but the stigma was still hard to overcome. The memories from Unity Dow are a good way to put faces on complicated and emotional problems and they’re supplemented by political and scientific commentary by Max Essex that can provide context and help you understand people’s situations and decisions.

Title: The Green Crow
Review: I immediately loved the main character and her possibly hallucinated crow. It also highlighted one of my many issues with mental health professionals—it’s hard to get help when you need it but after you’ve been diagnosed, everything can be associated with a symptom, even normal activities and feelings. I know that it’s hard to separate normal unpleasant feelings from the more harmful ones (having some experience in this area) but not everything needs to be pathologised. And in the case of this woman, she may have a psychological problem that predates her abusive husband, but he seems to be her main problem. If the psychiatric hospital is doing anything helpful for her, it seems to be mostly in giving her a reprieve from him. This story has also brought forward the ways in which men have used psychiatric problems, real or imagined, to manipulate and control women. It’s quite surrealist in places and a bit too plausible in others.

Title: The Book of Magic
Review: Such good fun, right from the start. I love these books. They always make me feel witchier and more adventurous.

Title: Sigil Witchery: A Witch's Guide to Crafting Magick Symbols
Review: Good fun and easy to get into. It’s a fun way to play with sigils and I think it’s probably accessible to non-artists. I will be doodling with more intentionality sometimes now. In addition to how to make them, it also includes quite a lot of creative ways to use them. I like that she encourages people to put aside the childhood bagage about not being able to draw and just try. It really does just take practice.

Title: Pure Colour
Review: An oddly beautiful philosophical story told in tiny moments and full of wonder. It has very little plot but focuses on how we define our relationships, how we can know other people or ourselves, and how we love people. It’s about loss and death but in the most radiant way. It hypothesises about second chances, second lives, and second worlds: cosmic do-overs. And sometimes, second deaths. It was also sometimes funny, not in a laugh-out-loud sort of way but in a smiling through the tears sort of way.

Title: Death Takes Me
Review:
Wow, that was weird! I knew it was a mystery but wasn’t sure what to expect. It turns out, it’s impossible to know what to expect! I was surprised by the weirdness at the beginning, but it got my attention. It’s anything but a normal detective story, all short sentences from two characters obsessed with poetry and ideas around expectation, gender and violence. I’m not sure I liked it but I did keep listening. 

I think it’s more allegory than crime novel but allegory for what I’m not sure. With the excessive number of penises, I think it’s trying to make a point about gendered violence and how female victims are treated by society, but I’m not sure what that point is. And something to do with Argentinian poet Alejandra Pizarnik that I didn’t understand at all until the essay that appeared halfway through the book. 

I don’t know if it’s the translation but the excessive use of sentence fragments, and sometimes just a bunch of single words hanging in the air, became quite grating. If she was going for the brevity and “crystalline prose” that Pizarnik admired, I’m not sure this is it. Ideas in sentence fragments might work in a 10-20 line prose poem, but in a novel, it doesn’t have at all the same effect and feels a bit like the novel went through the blender. 

The second half was much better than the first, or maybe I just got used to it, I’m not sure. But I still have no idea which I just read!

Title: Finding My Way
Review: It was good to read her perspective of growing up and becoming an adult separate from all the media and social media circuses. Sometimes I think too many people expect too much from one person, and not just about Malala, as though one person can solve all the world’s problems while absolving others from responsibility. That said, I do love her work around girls' education and I’m heartbroken and horrified for the Afghan girls who can’t go to school or live free in any way anymore. And I’m glad she’s gotten to go back to Pakistan sometimes despite all the death threats.

Title: The Thursday Murder Club
Review: I needed to read something more lighthearted after a couple other recent reads and, today, that was an irreverent murder mystery. It turned out to be delightful with more than a hint of Miss Marple, which I’ll never complain about. I loved this cast of characters and I’ll have to read the next one!

Title: The Seed Keeper
Review: Rosalie’s story is so moving. We really do need to find a way to live with the land in a healthier way but it’s hard to imagine ways to do that when you’re up against governments and multinational corporations. I suppose everyone just has to do what they can to live in a better way. Seeds really are tiny miracles and the soil and water give us life. There’s so much suffering in the world but we really don’t need to do this to each other.  This was an extraordinary book and the blurb just can’t do it justice.

Title: The Savage Detectives
Review: My first thought on reading this book was that it was most definitely written by a man. The first and third sections felt completely different from the largest second section which went on too long and took itself too seriously. I would have enjoyed it more if there were fewer characters to keep track of. The little glimpses into people’s lives were interesting and I liked parts of it but I didn’t love this book the way other people do.

Title: The Secret Place
Review: This was a fun mystery, although the way the teenage girls spoke and treated each other, while not inaccurate, was annoying. But I guess that can just be an annoying stage of life. It certainly didn’t make me nostalgic for junior high or high school, but nothing can do that! Overall, it was a fun mystery and a pretty good exploration of the precariousness of important friendships when big transitions happen.

Title: The Wind that Lays Waste
Review: This was a sharp little novella. It’s always frustrating to me to listen to preaching, even in fiction, but that’s religious trauma for you. I wanted that character to be more respectful to the others but he couldn’t see past his worldview, which often happens. It was a sparse and beautifully translated short book.
